At its core, the Ship of Theseus is about identity and change over time. Plutarch wrote about it: if you replace every single wooden plank of a ship piece by piece over the years, is it still the same ship? 

Philosophers usually split into two camps on this. One side says continuity wins—the form, function, and history keep it the same object, even if the material changes. The other side says an object *is* its parts, so if every part is swapped out, you've technically built a brand new ship. 

And it gets messier: what if someone gathered up all the discarded old planks and built a second ship out of them? Which one is the *real* Ship of Theseus then?
